S062.name: Specific_Phobic_Fear
S062.description: Marked fear or anxiety about a specific object or situation that is out of proportion to the actual danger. (Note: In children, may be expressed by crying, tantrums, freezing, or clinging).

subtypes.Animal Type: Marked fear of animals or insects like dogs, bees, snakes, or spiders.
subtypes.Natural Environment Type: Marked fear of the natural environment like storms, heights, water, or the dark.
subtypes.Blood-Injection-Injury Type: Marked fear of seeing blood, receiving injections, or medical procedures.
subtypes.Situational Type: Marked fear of specific situations like airplanes, elevators, tunnels, bridges, or enclosed spaces.
subtypes.Other Type: Marked fear of other situations like choking, vomiting, loud sounds, or costumed characters.

S063.name: Immediate_Fear/Anxiety_Response
S063.description: The phobic object or situation almost always provokes immediate fear or anxiety.

subtypes.Anticipatory Anxiety: Strong anxiety triggered just by thinking about the possibility of encountering the phobic object.
subtypes.Immediate Panic Response: Overwhelming fear erupting immediately upon facing the phobic object.
subtypes.Physiological Panic Symptoms: Intense physical reactions such as heart palpitations, shortness of breath, sweating, or trembling.
subtypes.Freezing: Feeling paralyzed or unable to move due to extreme fear.

S064.name: Phobic_Avoidance_Endure
S064.description: The phobic object or situation is actively avoided or endured with intense fear or anxiety.

subtypes.Active Avoidance: Intentionally and completely staying away from contact with the phobic object or situation.
subtypes.Functional Impairment due to Avoidance: Accepting severe restrictions on daily life, job, or social activities to avoid the phobic object.
subtypes.Enduring with Distress: Forcing oneself to endure the situation while experiencing intense fear and anxiety because it cannot be avoided.
subtypes.Reliance on Safety Signals: Barely enduring the exposure by relying on a companion or safety object.

symptom.disease_info: Specific Phobia is characterized by a persistent, excessive fear of a clearly circumscribed object or situation (e.g., animals, heights, flying, injections) that is out of proportion to the actual threat. Exposure almost invariably triggers marked fear or anxiety and leads to avoidance or intense distress, causing clinically significant interference in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning when the feared stimulus is encountered or anticipated. The course is often chronic if untreated, though many individuals structure their lives to minimize contact with the phobic trigger, delaying recognition until role demands change (e.g., new job requirements, caregiving roles, or travel). It is distinguished from other anxiety disorders by its narrow focus on a specific object/situation, absence of pervasive worry or unexpected panic attacks, and relative absence of fears about social evaluation or multiple domains.

patient.stressor: About seven months ago, Esteban’s clinic began a new outreach program that involved more home visits and community events, increasing his exposure to dogs in patients’ yards and at neighborhood gatherings. He had a long-standing discomfort around dogs from a childhood incident in Honduras when a neighbor’s dog chased and knocked him down, but he had mostly managed this by choosing routes and social situations where he rarely encountered them. With the new program, however, he found himself frequently needing to enter homes and backyards where dogs were present, leading him to reschedule visits, ask colleagues to cover certain houses, and avoid otherwise valuable community events in parks. When a respected elderly patient gently teased him about refusing a simple house call because of her small dog, he realized his fear was starting to compromise the care he wanted to provide and his reputation in the community, prompting him to seek psychiatric evaluation through a colleague’s referral.
patient.chief_complaint: “Whenever I know I might run into a dog, the moment I get near one I’m suddenly overwhelmed with fear and tension, even if it’s just a small pet.”

S062.name: Specific_Phobic_Fear
S062.description: Marked fear or anxiety about a specific object or situation that is out of proportion to the actual danger. (Note: In children, may be expressed by crying, tantrums, freezing, or clinging).
S062.manifestation: I know it sounds silly for a grown man and a doctor, but when I see a dog—even a little one on a leash—I instantly picture it jumping on me and biting like that dog did when I was a kid, and the fear I feel is way stronger than what I know makes sense for the situation.

S063.name: Immediate_Fear/Anxiety_Response
S063.description: The phobic object or situation almost always provokes immediate fear or anxiety.
S063.manifestation: These last months, any time I’m about to enter a house or yard on a visit and hear barking or see a dog, my chest tightens, my heart starts pounding, my hands get sweaty, and I feel this rush of dread like something bad is about to happen right then, even if the dog is behind a fence or the owner is holding it.

S064.name: Phobic_Avoidance_Endure
S064.description: The phobic object or situation is actively avoided or endured with intense fear or anxiety.
S064.manifestation: I’ve been rearranging my schedules, asking coworkers to take patients who have dogs, and skipping community events in the park, and when I can’t avoid it and have to go into a home with a dog, I’ll make the owner hold it or lock it away while I rush through the visit, the whole time feeling on edge and ready to bolt if it comes near me.

add_requirements.functional_impairment: Because of this fear, I’ve turned down or rescheduled several home visits, asked coworkers to cover patients with dogs, and skipped community events, which makes it harder for me to do my job properly and I worry it’s starting to affect how patients and colleagues see me.
add_requirements.duration: This has really flared up and become a steady problem over the last seven months, ever since our clinic started the new outreach program with more home visits where I might run into dogs.
